headline: Israel's vote was clean. Now the president picks.
summary: Israel's president took the certified results of last week's election on Wednesday and began asking party leaders who should form a government. Netanyahu's bloc won 53 of 120 seats, Gadi Eisenkot's 48, two Arab-led alliances 19. The commission found no evidence the vote was stolen, as Netanyahu's camp claimed. Herzog has several days to pick.

cover_question.q: Why isn't the most seats a win?

cover_answer: You need 61 of 120. Nobody has it, so the president picks.
table_question: If you got the most votes but not half, did you win?

5-7.chip: Bring it up if it fits the day
5-7.script: Israel had a big vote last week, and no side got enough seats to win on its own. The judges checked and said the vote was fair. Now the president is asking each group who they'd pick, and one leader gets 28 days to build a big enough team. Like picking teams at recess when nobody has enough players. The grown-ups have it.
5-7.why: Recess teams is a thing they do every day. Keep the stolen-vote shouting off this card; one loud word becomes the story.
5-7.why_long: A child this age takes one vivid feature for the whole event, so the script hands them recess teams with nobody holding enough players, and keeps the stolen-vote claims off the card; one loud word would become the story. Expect "why don't they just vote again?" They might, early next year, if nobody can build the team.

8-12.script: Israel's parliament has 120 seats and you need 61 to govern. Netanyahu's side won 53, Gadi Eisenkot's 48, two Arab-led groups 19, so nobody has it. Netanyahu's camp cried stolen; the commission found no evidence. The president, a referee after a draw, picks who tries for 61.
8-12.why: Seats they can add up, a referee who checks the claim, a clock. At this age they want to know the rule was applied.
8-12.why_long: This age is checking whether adults keep the rules, so the script gives them numbers they can add: 53, 48 and 19 against the 61 needed. Then the referee: the commission checked the stolen-vote claim and found nothing. Expect "what if nobody gets to 61?" A new election early next year, so the president told the parties to bend.

13-17.script: Netanyahu lost his majority and said Arab-led parties stole the vote. The commission found no evidence. What should happen to a leader who calls a clean vote stolen? Second: Arab-led parties won a record 19 seats, and all but one Jewish party vowed not to work with them. Position or problem?
13-17.why: Two true things: the claim was checked and failed, and 19 seats are sidelined. At this age they can hold both.
13-17.why_long: A teenager can hold two true things at once: the stolen-election claim was checked and found empty, and 19 seats won fairly are kept out of every coalition by promises made before the vote. The script hands them both. Expect "would you work with them?" Say what you think and why; they are testing whether you argue straight.

5-7.a: Nobody. One leader gets 28 days to build a big enough team.

8-12.q: Why isn't the most seats a win?
8-12.a: You need 61 of 120. With 53, the president picks who tries.
The commission checked every claim and found no evidence.

13-17.q: Why won't anyone work with the Arab parties?
13-17.a: All but one Jewish party promised not to, before the vote.

13-17.q: Can the president pick whoever he wants?
13-17.a: Mostly. He picks whoever he thinks can build a coalition.
